items.text:
Verified against the actual overlay source. Here's the verdict.

## Short answer

**Yes — the statement is true *for the purpose it claims* (getting the udev.netname overlay to rename the interface).** It's confirmed by both the overlay code and Miguel's empirical test. Shane is also right — but Shane and the PR are talking about two *different* 6-byte quantities, and the confusion in that thread comes from conflating them.

## Why it's true — the overlay does a literal suffix match

The template Miguel linked, [70-persistent-net.rules.ww](warewulf/overlays/udev.netname/rootfs/etc/udev/rules.d/70-persistent-net.rules.ww#L4-L5), renders this for an Infiniband-type netdev:

```
SUBSYSTEM=="net", ACTION=="add", ATTR{address}=="?*<hwaddr>", NAME="<device>"
```

The `?*` prefix is a udev glob (`?` = one char, `*` = any run), and the whole pattern must match the entire `ATTR{address}`. So this is a **suffix match**: whatever you put in `--hwaddr` just has to be the *trailing* portion of the full IPoIB address. The literal last 6 bytes are, by definition, a valid suffix → it matches. That's exactly why Miguel's "last 6 straight up + `--infiniband`" worked.

## The nuance the PR should be aware of

An IPoIB hardware address is **20 bytes**, not 6. Using your own doc's example ([infiniband.md](hpc-lab/docs/infiniband.md#L15) has GUID `0xf452140300f55431`):

```
80:00:00:66:fe:80:00:00:00:00:00:00:f4:52:14:03:00:f5:54:31   ← 20-byte address
                                     └──────── GUID (last 8) ────────┘
```

There are two distinct "6-byte" things people mean:

| Quantity | Value | What it's for |
|---|---|---|
| **Literal last 6 bytes** of the address | `14:03:00:f5:54:31` | ✅ the udev suffix match → **the PR's use case** |
| **48-bit IB "compatibility MAC"** = GUID with its 4th & 5th bytes removed | `f4:52:14:f5:54:31` | PXE boot / dnsmasq / dracut DHCP identity |

Shane's "not the last 6 bytes — it's the last 8 with the 4th and 5th removed" is describing the **compatibility MAC** (the EUI-64→EUI-48 conversion, dropping the `FF:FE`-position middle bytes). That is *not* a contiguous suffix, so it would **not** match this udev rule. But it's the right identifier for *booting* over IB — a different mechanism entirely.

So both are correct:
- **udev rename (the PR's scope):** literal last 6 bytes ✓ — and `6` specifically because `--hwaddr` is also emitted as a kernel arg, where dracut hardcodes a 6-byte length (Miguel hit exactly this).
- **Actually booting/DHCP off IB:** you'd need the compatibility MAC, not the last 6 bytes. Miguel's own closing caveat acknowledges this ("it merely has the right length… doesn't mean it would work for booting from it").

## Recommendation for the PR

The sentence is accurate as written, since it's explicitly scoped to "so that the udev.netname overlay can set the persistent interface name." If you want to preempt the exact confusion that happened in that Slack thread, consider a one-line clarification, e.g.:

> …set `--hwaddr` to the **literal last 6 bytes** of the interface's hardware address (the trailing 6 octets of the 20-byte IPoIB address — *not* the 48-bit InfiniBand compatibility MAC). This is sufficient for the udev overlay to rename the interface; it does not configure the node to PXE/DHCP-boot over InfiniBand.

Want me to check out the warewulf branch this PR is on and draft that edit, or is this just a review of Miguel's upstream PR (in which case I'd leave it as a review comment)?

items.text:
Quick byte refresher first, then the pasteable comment.

## The numbers

- **MAC address = 6 bytes** (48 bits)
- **IB GUID / EUI-64 = 8 bytes** (64 bits)
- **IPoIB hardware address = 20 bytes** (160 bits) — the GUID is the last 8 of these
- **MAC-48 → EUI-64 ("modified EUI-64")**: insert `FF:FE` between the first 3 bytes (OUI) and the last 3 bytes:

  ```
  AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF   →   AA:BB:CC:FF:FE:DD:EE:FF
   1  2  3  4  5  6         1  2  3  4  5  6  7  8
                                  ↑ FF:FE sits in byte positions 4 and 5
  ```

So going the other way (GUID → 48-bit compatibility MAC) you **drop bytes 4 and 5** — exactly Shane's "last 8 with the 4th and 5th removed." That gives a non-contiguous result, which is why it is *not* the same as the literal trailing 6 bytes the udev rule matches on.

---

## Complete comment / suggestion to paste

Since you're reviewing Miguel's PR, here's a self-contained review comment. The `suggestion` block replaces the original Note; the text under it explains the reasoning for other reviewers.

````markdown
This is accurate for the udev rename, but the phrase "last 6 bytes" tripped up the
Slack discussion, so it's worth disambiguating. Suggested wording:

```suggestion
**Note:** If, once you boot the nodes, you find that the IB interface was
renamed to something other than ib0 and hence not assigned the given IP, you
can fix it by setting `--type="Infiniband"` and `--hwaddr` to the **literal
last 6 bytes** of the interface's hardware address — i.e. the trailing 6 octets
of the 20-byte IPoIB address, *not* the 48-bit InfiniBand "compatibility MAC".
The `udev.netname` overlay renders a wildcard suffix match
(`ATTR{address}=="?*<hwaddr>"`), so those trailing 6 bytes are all it needs to
set the persistent interface name. (This is enough to rename the interface; it
does not by itself make the node PXE/DHCP-boot over InfiniBand, which uses the
compatibility MAC as the client identifier.)
```

Rationale — there are two different 6-ish-byte quantities and it's easy to conflate them:

- A **MAC** is 6 bytes; an **IB GUID** is 8 bytes; the full **IPoIB hardware address** is 20 bytes (the GUID is its last 8).
- The **48-bit compatibility MAC** is the GUID with bytes **4 and 5 removed** (the `FF:FE` positions of a modified-EUI-64). That's what matters at PXE/DHCP boot — but it's *non-contiguous*, so it would **not** match this overlay's rule.
- The overlay ([`70-persistent-net.rules.ww`](https://github.com/warewulf/warewulf/blob/main/overlays/udev.netname/rootfs/etc/udev/rules.d/70-persistent-net.rules.ww)) matches `?*<hwaddr>` — a plain **suffix** — so the *literal* last 6 bytes of the address are a valid match, which is what @miguel confirmed empirically. 6 specifically because `--hwaddr` is also emitted as a kernel arg where dracut hardcodes a 6-byte length.
````
